notes.meaning: The people of Judah chose Josiah's younger son Jehoahaz to be their new king after Josiah died in battle. They anointed him quickly, preferring him over his older brother Eliakim.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that the Chronicler gives no moral judgment on Jehoahaz, letting his brief kingship simply fade out to leave room for the future restored Davidic line.

notes.meaning: Jehoahaz ruled for only three months in 609 BC before his reign was cut short. He did not follow his father's godly example, and his short rule quickly ended in disaster.
Pharaoh Neco of Egypt removed Jehoahaz from the throne to show that Judah was now under Egyptian control. He forced the nation to pay a heavy fine of silver and gold as a sign of surrender.
Pharaoh Neco placed Eliakim on the throne and changed his name to Jehoiakim to prove he had full authority over him. He then dragged Jehoahaz away as a prisoner to Egypt, where he later died.

Jehoiakim ruled for eleven years, but he turned away from God and led the nation back into wicked practices. He taxed the people heavily and ruled selfishly instead of continuing his father Josiah's reforms.
King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon marched against Jerusalem and took control of Judah. He put Jehoiakim in bronze chains with the intent to haul him away to Babylon as a captive.

Nebuchadnezzar took sacred vessels and furnishings from the temple in Jerusalem and placed them in the temple of his own false god in Babylon. This began the stripping of God's house by foreign conquerors.
Jehoiakim's long record of idolatry and unjust rule was well known and recorded in the royal annals. When his troubled reign ended, his young son Jehoiachin took the throne.
Jehoiachin became king as a teenager and ruled for only three months and ten days. Like his father, he did evil in God's eyes during his brief time on the throne.

In the spring, Nebuchadnezzar summoned Jehoiachin and carried him off to Babylon, along with more precious items from the temple. The Babylonian king then appointed Jehoiachin's uncle Zedekiah to rule Judah in his place.
Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he was placed on the throne, and he reigned for eleven years. He would be the final king of David's royal line to rule from Jerusalem before the city fell.
Zedekiah chose to do evil rather than obey the Lord who had put him in power. God sent the prophet Jeremiah to guide him, but the king refused to humble his heart and listen to God's warnings.
Zedekiah had sworn a solemn oath of loyalty to Nebuchadnezzar in God's name, but he broke that promise and rebelled. His stubborn refusal to repent closed his heart against turning back to the Lord.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Traditional Catholic scholarship notes that Nebuchadnezzar was relatively lenient, making Zedekiah's treaty-breaking ingratitude especially offensive, which brought harsh consequences upon Jerusalem.

notes.meaning: The priests and the people followed the bad example of their kings and completely abandoned true worship. They adopted the corrupt religious rituals of pagan neighbors and brought filthy idolatry right into God's holy temple.
God did not leave His people without warnings, but sent prophets to them early and often. He did this out of deep pity for His people and love for the place where His name was honored.
Instead of listening, the people ridiculed God's messengers and laughed at His warnings. Their repeated rejection finally exhausted God's patience until judgment became unavoidable.

God allowed the Babylonian army to invade Jerusalem and bring terrible destruction upon the city. The soldiers showed no mercy to anyone, killing young and old alike even inside the holy sanctuary where people had fled for safety.
The invaders gathered all the remaining treasures from the temple, along with the wealth of the king and his royal officials. Everything of value was carried off to Babylon as spoil of war.
The Babylonian soldiers set fire to the temple of God and tore down the defensive stone walls of Jerusalem. They burned every palace and reduced the glorious city and its finest treasures to ruins.

The survivors of the slaughter were marched off as captives to Babylon, where they lived as servants to the Babylonian rulers. They remained in exile for decades until the Persian empire rose and conquered Babylon.

The land was left empty and unplowed for seventy years, just as the prophet Jeremiah had foretold. This long desolation made up for all the Sabbath rest years that the people had refused to give the land during their centuries of disobedience.

In his very first year over the empire, King Cyrus of Persia issued an official decree to all his subjects. God stirred the Persian king's heart to make this announcement so that His ancient promise through Jeremiah would come true.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Historical scholars observe that Cyrus attributed his conquests and decrees to the Babylonian god Marduk on the Cyrus Cylinder, while the biblical writers recognize the Lord as the true mover of his heart.

notes.meaning: Cyrus announced that the Lord, the God of heaven, had given him dominion over the nations and commissioned him to rebuild the temple in Jerusalem. He invited any of God's people to journey back home with the Lord's blessing, ending the book with fresh hope of restoration.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars highlight that while the Book of Kings ends in Babylonian exile without a resolution, Chronicles intentionally closes on a hopeful note by looking ahead to the rebuilt temple.
